cognates.gloss: cud brought up to be chewed again

evidence.locator: Book I p. 400, n5382, form VIII
C01258, Targum Isa 17:6 and Palestinian Targum Deu 32:14
pp. 96–97, ǧarǧīr, with an example from spoken Palestinian Arabic

cognates.gloss: part of an animal, possibly its gullet

evidence.locator: G, s.v. gaggurītu, variant gangurītu, Hg. D 46 and Hg. B IV 43

note:
Jer.30.23 has several possible root assignments in the corpus. The storm and the following verb support a sweeping or whirling movement. The connection between drawing a load, drawing up cud and sawing remains uncertain. The homonymous weight is under gerah and the olive fruit under gargar. Gerar is a place name of uncertain derivation.

Added 2026-11-21: גַּרְגַּר, from its former one-word entry. Filed under the geminate root גרר as its reduplicated form (*gargar), like גַּרְגְּרוֹת 'throat'; the link to dragging is not clear, and the berry may be named for its small round grains.

Its former note: The Levantine Arabic term specifically describes a shriveled olive and may have entered the dialect through Aramaic. Isaiah describes the few fruits still on the branches without saying that they are shriveled.

Added 2026-11-21: גַּרְגְּרוֹת, from its former one-word entry. Filed under the geminate root גרר as its reduplicated form: Arabic جَرْجَرَ is a camel's repeated cry in its windpipe and the sound of drink in the throat (Lane p. 400), and Hebrew גֵּרָה 'cud' of the same root is brought up through the throat.

Its former note: The Syriac and Mandaic forms refer to the throat and can name internal anatomy. The four Hebrew passages present the neck as the place for an ornament. The Akkadian term is less secure because its precise anatomical referent is unknown.
summary: Habakkuk pictures a conqueror dragging captives in a fishing net. The dietary laws use the same consonants for bringing up the cud. A saw and the stones cut with it form another pair in the account of Solomon’s building work. Isaiah compares the survivors to the few olives still hanging on a tree after its branches have been beaten. Proverbs pictures instruction worn around the neck like a pendant. The image gives wisdom a place both on the body and in the heart.

senses.definition: Pull someone or something along by force.

evidence.note: The conqueror drags people in his net like a fisherman hauling a catch.
The violence of the wicked drags them away.

senses.definition: Bring previously swallowed food back up for chewing.

evidence.note: The pig has a divided hoof but does not bring up the cud.

senses.definition: Be cut by drawing a saw through the material.

evidence.note: The costly stones were sawn to measure on both their inner and outer faces.
The participle characterises Yahweh’s storm, which whirls down upon the wicked.

senses.definition: Food brought back up into the mouth to be chewed again.

evidence.note: Bringing up cud and having a divided hoof are the paired signs in the food law.
The camel exemplifies the first sign alone.
The pig exemplifies the divided hoof alone.
The two signs are restated together.
The camel, hare and rock hyrax are grouped by their chewing.
The pig is again described as lacking the chewing sign.

senses.definition: A cutting tool used on building stone and listed with iron implements.

evidence.note: The implement cuts dressed stones to their specified dimensions.
Saws appear with picks and axes after the capture of Rabbah.
The parallel account names saws among the implements.

senses.definition: Pull a person along by force.

evidence.note: Paul is dragged outside Lystra after being stoned.

senses.definition: A place named in the description of the Canaanite boundary and the seat of Abimelech.

evidence.note: Gerar gives the direction of travel from Sidon in the boundary description, just as Sodom does in the following clause.
Abimelech is called king of Gerar.

words.summary: Gerar is a place name. Its connection to the verb גָּרַר is uncertain.

senses.definition: An individual fruit of the olive tree, counted among the gleanings on its branches.

evidence.note: Two or three fruits remain at the very top, and four or five on the fruitful branches. The comparison names the tree as an olive.

senses.definition: The part of the body around which a pendant or necklace hangs. Proverbs uses the plural form for one person’s neck.

evidence.note: A garland goes on the head and pendants around the neck.
The pupil binds loyal love and faithfulness around the neck and writes them on the heart.
Wisdom and discretion adorn the neck.
The parents’ teaching is bound on the heart and tied around the neck.
